Question: Of \(28\) students taking at least one subject the number taking Mathematics and English only equals the number taking Mathematics only. No student takes English only or History only, and six students take Mathematics and History, but no English. The number taking English and History only is five times the number taking all three subjects. If the number taking all three subjects is even and non-zero, the number taking English and Mathematics only is:
Solution:
Group students by exactly which subjects they take, so that each student is counted once. Let \(m\) be the number taking Mathematics only; the number taking Mathematics and English only is also \(m\). Let \(t\) be the number taking all three subjects, where \(t\) is a positive even integer.

The possibly nonempty groups have sizes \(m,m,6,5t,t\): Mathematics only, Mathematics and English only, Mathematics and History only, English and History only, and all three. English only and History only contribute zero. These groups cover all 28 students without overlap, so
\[
2m+6+5t+t=28,
\qquad m+3t=11.
\]
Because \(m\geq0\), we have \(t\leq11/3\). The only positive even integer in this range is \(t=2\). Hence
\[
m=11-3(2)=5.
\]
These counts are feasible: \(5+5+6+10+2=28\). Therefore the number taking English and Mathematics only is \(\boxed{5}\), choice A.
